# Continual-ARC lesson: edge bars and rays

Observed across demos in task-e965a108 (confirmed test submission):

- Background is a uniform color. Short contiguous bars along opposing grid edges define edge-ray bands. Sparse pixels in another color specify which inward rays are active and their color.
- For each sparse marker, draw a straight ray perpendicular to the edge bar from the corresponding edge toward the marker. Fill background cells along that ray with the marker's original color; recolor the marker itself to 4. Do not continue past the marker. The edge-bar cells remain unchanged.
- The marker's offset within its edge band identifies the corresponding ray in the opposing edge band; draw that parallel ray inward across the grid in the same marker color when there is no stopping marker on it. Unselected offsets stay background. Keep positions exact; do not indiscriminately paint every cell in a stripe.
- Example confirmed: 25x6 grid, background 6, edge color 3 bars at right rows 0-3 and left rows 19-22; markers color 7 at (r20,c3),(r21,c4),(r22,c2). Output unchanged except: top rows r1-r3 get 7 in c0-c4 (right-edge rays at matching offsets); bottom r20 fills c1-c2 with 7 and changes c3 to 4; r21 fills c1-c3 with 7 and changes c4 to 4; r22 fills c1 with 7 and changes c2 to 4. All edge 3 cells and all other 6s remain unchanged.
- Avoid extrapolating color changes from unrelated isolated cells: markers become 4, fill is the marker color (here 7), and edge color stays intact.

This is a compact observation, not a complete formal rule. Validate each candidate against all demos and carefully map row/column offsets before submitting.

# Continual-ARC observed transformation

## Rule from solved instance task-89695a26
For an input grid `G` of height `H` and width `W`, create output of size `3H x 2W`:

1. For each source row, horizontally reflect it and concatenate the original row: `row[::-1] + row`.
2. Stack rows with source-row indices `H-1 ... 0`, then `0 ... H-1`, then `H-1 ... 0` (vertical sequence = vertically flipped grid, original grid, vertically flipped grid).

Equivalently, vertically concatenate `flip_vertical(G), G, flip_vertical(G)`, then mirror each row horizontally and concatenate the unmirrored row.

Verified against demos: 3x13 -> 9x26 and 8x1 -> 24x2. Test 10x14 -> 30x28. The first submission used a mistaken vertical index pattern; corrected order above yielded a correct answer.

# Continual-ARC solved task notes

## task-92aa891e — repeat the final panel

Observed test: 20x7 grid with background 2 and full-width separator rows of 3 at row indices 6 and 13. This forms three 6-row panels separated by 1-row dividers. The non-background pattern appears in the last panel (rows 14–19). Correct output copied that 6x7 panel into each of the three panels at identical local row/column positions, leaving separator rows unchanged.

General rule supported by the demo: identify equal-sized panels separated by full-line dividers; copy the populated panel's pattern across the other panels without changing local coordinates or colors. Demo had vertical divider 3 and horizontal divider 3 forming repeated regions; foreground colors 6/7 were copied while backgrounds stayed the same. For this instance, preserve background 2, separator 3, and copy all non-2 markings from the final six-row panel into the earlier panels.

# Continual-ARC observations

## Hollow frames and singleton markers (observed task-9a8c4ac8)
Demo established: on an 8 background, hollow rectangular/square outlines (e.g. 5x5 frames in colors 1 and 4) are filled in their interiors with color 7. The outlines and surrounding background remain unchanged. A separate 3x3 outline/object in color 5 with a single center background cell is likewise filled at its center with 7; its border/background remain unchanged. In the test, fill the 3x3 interior of the 5-colored 5x5 frame with 7, and fill the center cell of the separate 3x3 9-colored outline with 7. This exact transformation solved the instance.

Generalizable heuristic: when objects are hollow frames or enclosed background cells, check demos for a consistent interior fill color (here 7); preserve all outlines and other cells. This is an observed pattern, not a guaranteed rule for every task.

# Continual-ARC task pattern: tiled grid with colored lattice markers

## Observed solved instance
Task id `task-1303b937` was solved with output:

```json
[[2,2,2,7],[6,2,2,2],[2,2,2,2],[2,1,2,8]]
```

The input was a regular lattice of compartments: background/interior fill 2; lattice lines color 3; special marker colors on grid-line endpoints/intersections. Lattice boundaries were at rows `0,5,10,15,20` and columns `0,6,12,18,24`, making a 4x4 set of compartments. Most output cells keep the compartment interior fill (2). A compartment is recolored when its four corner lattice points carry the same special color:
- rows 0–5, cols 18–24: four corners are 7 => output row 0 col 3 = 7
- rows 5–10, cols 0–6: four corners are 6 => output row 1 col 0 = 6
- rows 15–20, cols 6–12: four corners are 1 => output row 3 col 1 = 1
- rows 15–20, cols 18–24: four corners are 8 => output row 3 col 3 = 8

## Demonstration evidence
A demo had interior fill 8, grid lines 6, and a 27x23 input. Its output was 6x3:
`[[5,8,8],[8,8,8],[2,8,8],[8,8,8],[8,8,8],[8,8,5]]`.
Grid row lines at 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22,25 and column lines at 1,8,15,22. Recolored cells matched four equal corners: marker 5 at rows 4&7, cols 1&8 -> first output row/col; marker 2 at rows 10&13, cols 1&8 -> third output row/col; marker 5 at rows 19&22, cols 15&22 -> last output row/col. This suggests output includes the rectangular subarray of compartments from the minimum to maximum special-marker lattice coordinates, cropping unmarked outer bands (here rows 1–4 and 22–25), while retaining fill color in cells inside that bounding extent.

## Useful solving procedure for recurrences
1. Identify the repeated lattice spacing, grid-line coordinates, and each compartment's interior fill color.
2. Interpret each potential output cell as a compartment between adjacent horizontal and vertical lattice lines; start with its interior fill.
3. If all four lattice corner values of a compartment are the same special (non-gridline) color, set that output cell to that color; otherwise leave its fill.
4. Determine whether the output is cropped to the compartment rectangle spanning the special-marker coordinates. The demo indicates it can crop marker-free outer bands; the solved test included the full 4x4 span because markers reached the extreme boundary lines.

Caution: First two attempted outputs were wrong; the third output above was confirmed correct. Do not confuse the dimensions of the compartment matrix with the number of exceptional markers. The first demo output was 6x3 despite the full lattice having additional unmarked outer bands.

# Continual-ARC task-9a8c4ac8: fill hollow squares by border side parity

Observed rule: Preserve the grid and all outlines; fill only the enclosed background cells of each hollow square. Use color 7 when the square's outer side length is odd, and color 2 when its outer side length is even. Background in examples is 3, but identify enclosed interior relative to each outline rather than assuming another color.

Evidence:
- Demo 1: 7x7 outline (color 0) interior filled 7; 3x3 outline (color 4) interior filled 7.
- Demo 2: 6x6 outline (color 0) interior filled 2; 7x7 outline (color 9) interior filled 7.
- Demo 3: 7x7 (color 8) -> 7; 6x6 (color 1) -> 2; 4x4 (color 8) -> 2; 6x6 (color 1) -> 2.
- Test solved: 4x4 outline color 4 -> interior 2; 7x7 outline color 1 -> interior 7; 3x3 outline color 8 -> interior 7.

Practical caution: submit exact grid dimensions; prior incorrect submissions were rejected as invalid due to malformed row lengths. Preserve every non-interior cell unchanged. For this 21x18 test, successful output used only the three interior fills above.

- The exact general mapping from line marks to output positions was not fully reconstructed in this instance. The only fully certain mapping for the 30x30 case is output `[[4]]`.

# Continual-ARC task notes

## Pairwise overlap / common-color separator puzzle

Evidence from task-01f3a263, solved and confirmed correct:

- A grid has two equal-size panels separated by a solid line (separator color may vary, e.g. full horizontal row of 5 or vertical column of 8/7).
- Align the panels cell-for-cell across the separator.
- Identify the color shared as the panels' patterned foreground/background color. Output the shared/common value at positions where both aligned input cells have that same value; use the shared color as output background elsewhere, and use color 3 for the overlap marks.
- In the confirmed test, horizontal separator 5 split two 10x13 panels. The common color was 2 (upper panel colors 2/6, lower 1/2). Correct output was 10x13, with 3 exactly where upper AND lower cells were both 2, and 2 elsewhere.

Demo checks validating the rule: vertical split demo with common color 2 produced 3 at pairwise 2/2 matches; a second vertical split with common color 6 produced 3 at pairwise 6/6 matches and 6 elsewhere. Thus don't invert one panel or mark a single-panel feature; find the shared color and take its cellwise intersection. Preserve panel orientation and dimensions; remove the separator.

## Hollow rectangle interior fill task (task-9a8c4ac8)
Observed rule from two demos and a correct test: find each axis-aligned, single-color rectangular outline with a hollow interior; fill the interior uniformly according to its interior dimensions/parity. Every tested interior with both dimensions even (2x2 or 4x4) was filled with color 2. Every tested interior with both dimensions odd (1x1, 3x3, or 5x5) was filled with color 7. Keep border and background unchanged. This solved the provided test (4x4 outer frames -> 2x2 holes filled 2; 5x5 outer frames -> 3x3 holes filled 7).

Examples: demo 1: 4x4 outer frames, 2x2 holes -> 2; 3x3 frame, 1x1 hole -> 7. Demo 2 confirms 2x2 and 4x4 holes -> 2; 1x1 and 5x5 holes -> 7. The precise generalization beyond observed sizes is not guaranteed; use demonstrations if a new instance's dimensions/parity do not match these cases.

A demo showed a 6×8 grid mapping to an 18×16 grid (height ×3, width ×2). The 18×16 output was vertically structured as three 6-row bands: rows 0–5, 6–11, and 12–17; the middle band reversed the row order of the first band, and the third repeated the first band. # Continual-ARC task 3caaa5de — copy a colored shape into matching background slots

Confirmed task rule from one demo and a correct test submission:

- Preserve the whole input grid, including the original colored template/object and all background cells.

# Continual-ARC lesson: full color remapping on noisy sparse grids

In task `task-0af76fdb`, the entire grid was transformed by a pointwise color map, not just the sparse markers. Two demos established distinct mappings:

- Demo 1: input background 3 and sparse markers 5; output maps `3 -> 0`, `5 -> 3`.
- Demo 2: input background 5 and sparse markers 1; output maps `5 -> 1`, `1 -> 0`.
- The test used the same palette arrangement as demo 2, so the correct output maps every 5 to 1 and every 1 to 0, preserving dimensions and positions.

Takeaway: do not infer a universal rule like “background becomes 0” or “marker becomes the background color.” Extract a complete input-color-to-output-color mapping from each demo; use the demo matching the test's palette and verify all cells/dimensions. A wrong palette assumption led to three incorrect submissions before applying the mapping from demo 2.

# Continual-ARC diagonal extension lesson (observed 2026-10-21)

Observed task rule from two demonstrations and a correctly solved test: if a monochrome diagonal stroke has at least two contiguous same-color cells on a uniform background, continue that stroke in its diagonal orientation through background cells in both directions. Stop at the grid boundary or at an existing non-background cell. Preserve all original colored cells and all other cells. Do not mistake adjacent unlike-color cells (including vertical/horizontal pairs) for lines to extend; in the demonstrated examples only the monochrome diagonal runs were extended. The solved test's 9s formed a down-right diagonal; extending that line while preserving the adjacent 1s and 5 correctly solved the grid.

Practical steps: identify same-color diagonal connected pairs/runs; derive the slope from the run; extend one step at a time in both directions while the target is background; stop before any non-background cell or outside the grid; construct and verify dimensions and original cells. Avoid guessing that all visible pairs should be extended; compare the direction-specific patterns across demos.

Note: attempted to update the continual-arc Workshop skill, but the Workshop tool refused repair because it reported the skill was not used in this run. This note is a workspace reference instead, not a published skill update.

# Continual-ARC learnings

## Horizontal alternating marker runs
A demonstrated transformation maps repeated 1D marker sequences with single background gaps to an alternating filled run, e.g. `8 0 8 0 8` -> `8 2 8 2 8`. In the solved test, the same rule applied to every horizontal run of 8s separated by exactly one 9: replace only those intervening 9s with 2, preserve all markers and all other cells. Inspect rowwise; do not change gaps larger than one cell or unrelated rows. Confirm every row retains exact dimensions before submitting. One demo was enough to infer the color and gap rule.

Caution: manually composing 27x15 grids caused errors (the first guess filled the wrong gaps; another output was rejected as invalid dimensions). Better to construct transformation programmatically or carefully validate row lengths and coordinates. The accepted result matched the simple criterion: for each adjacent pair of 8s in a row, if their columns differ by 2, color the cell between them 2.

# Continual-ARC: recolor line gaps between marker cells

Reusable pattern learned from task-eb4a14e3 (solved, after 5 wrong submissions):

## Rule
For each row and each column, find occurrences of the same marker color. For every pair of *consecutive* marker occurrences in that line, recolor the cells strictly between them that have the line's background/majority color to `3`. Keep both marker endpoints unchanged, and leave any other colors unchanged. Process rows and columns independently using the original input; the output is the union of those changes. Equivalent: a background-color cell becomes `3` if there is a marker of the same color somewhere before and after it in its row OR column, with no intervening marker needed beyond pairing consecutive occurrences.

This was verified against all 8 provided demonstrations, and the test grid was solved correctly with the rule. Demonstrations included: `1` gaps between `0` markers; `5` gaps between `2`; `2` gaps between `0`/`1`; `7` gaps between `8`; `5` gaps between `0`; and `6` gaps between `0`. The marker/background colors vary between instances, so infer which repeated sparse/marker color is acting as endpoints from the demo; do not assume fixed colors. In task-eb4a14e3's test, markers were `2`, background was `0`, and the intervening zeros became `3`.

## Implementation sketch
```python
out = [row[:] for row in grid]
# marker and background are inferred from the instance/demo
for each row r:
    positions = [c for c if grid[r][c] == marker]
    for x, y in consecutive_pairs(positions):
        for c in range(x+1, y):
            if grid[r][c] == background: out[r][c] = 3
for each column c:
    positions = [r for r if grid[r][c] == marker]
    for x, y in consecutive_pairs(positions):
        for r in range(x+1, y):
            if grid[r][c] == background: out[r][c] = 3
```

## Pitfalls learned
- Do not recolor the marker endpoints.
- Do not recolor marker-colored runs merely because they are bounded by background; that was a false hypothesis and caused wrong submissions.
- Do not recolor all cells between markers indiscriminately; only recolor the background color, preserving other colors.
- Include both horizontal and vertical spans. Intersections are simply set to `3` once.
- Use the original input for marker positions and fill eligibility so horizontal/vertical mutations do not affect later scans.
- Validate code against at least one full demo before submitting; printing/serializing output via a script minimizes transcription mistakes.

# Continual-ARC observations

## Puzzle family: colored line enclosures / fill pockets

Observed in task-c8726d19 (Oct 20, 2026): grids have a uniform background (examples: 5, 8, 9, 2) and thin/wide orthogonal line segments in a second color (examples: 1, 9, 8). The transformation preserves the line and background cells, and fills selected background pocket(s) with color 4.

### Demonstrated examples
- Demo 1: background 5, outline 1; fill a 2x3 interior cavity with 4.
- Demo 2: background 8, outline 9; fill interiors of two 2x3 rectangular cavities with 4.
- Demo 3: background 5, outline 1; fill the 2x4 pocket enclosed by the line shape with 4.
- Demo 4: background 9, outline 0; fill multiple pockets of differing sizes with 4 (including 2x3 and other small holes). Preserve all outline cells.
- Test: background 2, outline 8; correct output filled exactly rows 5–8, columns 22–24 (0-indexed) with 4, retaining all other cells. This is the 4x3 pocket bounded above by row 4, below by row 9, and on the left by the stepped outline; the canvas right edge closes it. Similar-looking regions elsewhere were not filled.

### Practical approach
1. Treat the non-background line color as walls; identify enclosed background pockets formed by connected orthogonal outline segments, sometimes using the grid boundary as a side.
2. Fill only the clearly enclosed pocket(s) with 4; preserve all wall cells and all other background. Do not assume every area at a corner or every background component is a fill target—the test had other visually plausible regions that remained unchanged.
3. Carefully trace all four sides and any openings before submitting. Prefer asking for another demo when ambiguity remains; incorrect submissions and demos each cost 1, while an unsolved instance costs 16.

Caution: these observations are from a small number of demonstrations and one solved test, so do not overgeneralize the precise enclosure/boundary rule without checking the current grid and examples.

# Continual-ARC observations

## Ray / boundary-pair transformation (task-e965a108)

Observed rule from two demos and one solved test: paired identical cells on an outer edge act as directional ray emitters along the inward perpendicular axis. A single differently colored cell on a ray's path is the target: fill the ray cells with the singleton's original color, and change that singleton to 4. Rays from edge pairs with no singleton in their path continue across the grid to the opposite edge; the pair cells themselves remain unchanged. In the solved instance, output preserved the edge pairs and background, painted the rays color 1, and changed the singleton 1 to 4.

Evidence/details:
- Demo 1: background 7; color-8 pair at top edge columns 14–15 emitted down column 14 to the bottom, in color 3; bottom edge pair columns 9–10 emitted up column 9 to a singleton 3 at row 3, which became 4; cells between pair and singleton were painted 3.

This indicates ray orientation is set by boundary pair geometry; rays carry the singleton/target color, and the ray's origin/target marker changes to 4.
- Solved test (22x18, background 9): pair of 0s at top row cols 3–4 and bottom row cols 16–17; singleton 1 at row 5 col 3. Output painted col 3 rows 1–4 as 1, converted singleton at (5,3) to 4, and painted col 16 rows 0–20 as 1; all other cells and pairs stayed as input.

# Continual-ARC reusable pattern notes

## Mirrored-row expansion with vertical bounce (observed demo)

Given an H×W input grid, this transformation produces a (3H)×(2W) output.

1. For each selected input row, form a 2W-wide row by concatenating its horizontal reversal with the original row: `reverse(row) + row`.
2. The output uses three vertical blocks of input rows: bottom-to-top order, top-to-bottom order, then bottom-to-top order. In zero-based source-row indices this is:
   `H-1, ..., 0, 0, ..., H-1, H-1, ..., 0`.
   Thus each block has H rows and adjacent blocks repeat their boundary row.
3. This was directly verified on a 7×7 demo → 21×14 output and solved a 2×14 test → 6×28 output. For the test, the row-source sequence was `[1,0,0,1,1,0]`; each row was reversed and then appended to itself.

When this pattern is suspected, use the demo dimensions and compare the first and last halves of output rows against reversed/original input rows before submitting. The task may use another rule despite similar dimensions, so verify against all available demos.

# Continual-ARC notes

## Pattern-stamping task family (observed 2026-10-20)

In these examples, a large grid has a background color, one compact colored template, and isolated singleton markers elsewhere. Preserve the original template. Stamp its non-background cells at each marker, aligning the template's center/central distinguished cell to the marker; leave the template-background cells transparent. The marker is overwritten by the template cell's color.

Evidence:
- Demo 2: three horizontal 8s form a 1x3 template; each isolated 1 receives a copy centered on it (center cell replaces 1 with 8).
- Demo 1: a 5x3 multicolor template is copied at the lone 0; the central 8 template cell aligns with/overwrites the 0.
- Solved test task-016ffa36: preserve the 4x5 multicolor template at rows 5–8, cols 5–9 (0-indexed); copy it around each isolated 8, aligning the central 0 at template offset (2,2) to that marker. Template background-colored cells remain background. Markers were at (4,19), (5,13), (9,20), (13,7), (14,17).

Practical checks: identify the template bounding box and its background; locate each singleton marker; infer the most central template cell as anchor (for even dimensions, use the distinguished/central cell indicated by the pattern); translate the template without clipping or altering its source; verify output dimensions and preserve all unrelated cells.

# Continual-ARC observations

## Task family: scatter markers + sample motif

Observed solved instance `task-016ffa36` (3 wrong attempts; two demos).

When a grid has a distinctive small colored motif and multiple isolated marker cells (here marker color 6), remove/replace each marker by a translated copy of the motif, preserving the rest of the background. ## Horizontal separator / overlap-mask task (observed task-de03619c)

When an ARC input consists of an upper binary mask (nonzero color, here `1` or `3`), a single full-width separator row, and a lower binary pattern (nonzero color, here `9` or `8`), pair rows above and below the separator in order. ## task-015a084f (solved)
Observed a grid with large uniform colored regions/rectangles (e.g. 5, 9, 3) on a uniform background, plus scattered single-cell anomalies in assorted colors (e.g. 0, 1, 4, 6, 7, 8). Output removes these anomalous pixels by restoring the color of the region/background they interrupt: isolated speckles on background become the background color; speckles embedded in a solid region become that region's color. # Continual-ARC learned rule: binary-panel intersection

Observed in task-de03619c (solved): An input contains two equal-sized binary panels separated by a full divider line/column in a third color. One panel has foreground color A and zero background; the other has foreground color B and zero background. The output is a single panel the same dimensions as either half, where each cell is foreground color 2 iff both corresponding input cells are nonzero; otherwise it is 0. Equivalently, take the cellwise AND/overlap of the two foreground masks and recolor overlap to 2.

Evidence from demos: horizontally stacked panels divided by a full row of 5; top sparse 4/6 foreground AND bottom 6/1 mask, output only overlaps recolored to 2. In the test, panels were side-by-side divided by a full column of 6, left 9-mask AND right 7-mask, output 27x14 of 2s at overlaps and 0 elsewhere.

When solving similar tasks: identify divider and the two same-sized panels; orientation determines split; output has half the input's width or height. Align cells at same local coordinates, preserve only overlap, map overlap to 2. Do not copy a panel alone or simply recolor all its nonzero cells.

## Hollow-frame fill rule (observed task `task-9a8c4ac8`, 2026-10-20)

Input contains several hollow rectangular frames against a uniform background; frame shapes and colors vary. Preserve the whole grid and each frame border. Fill every cell strictly inside each frame (the rectangular enclosed region) with a size-parity color:

Observed on task `task-2dc37cc6` (solved with 0 wrong submissions, 2 demo requests).

When a grid is partitioned by solid separator rows/columns, a populated tile may be the template and the task is to repeat that tile in each matching partition. - The task adds color 2 in straight horizontal/vertical gaps between existing pixels of the same non-background marker color. Existing marker pixels stay unchanged; unrelated background stays unchanged.

## Rule
The input is partitioned into a regular grid of 3×3 pixel tiles. The output has one cell per tile (input dimensions divided by 3). Each tile has background/noise pixels (often a mixture of 0 and 5, and in another demo primarily 5) and may contain a signal color. Decode each tile to the signal color present in it; output 0 if the tile contains no signal color. Do **not** output the most frequent color of the tile: the random/noisy background may have a local majority of 5, but such a tile still decodes to 0.

Identify signal colors from demonstrations as colors used for the embedded marks/shapes, distinct from the tile background/noise palette. In the examples here, demo 1 used 5 as background and other colors as signals (with 0 used as the empty output); demo 2 used a noisy 0/5 background and 2/3 as signal colors. The test's signal color was 4. Check every tile for the signal; even sparse signal marks encode their color. Preserve tile row/column order in the output.

## Rule / reusable pattern
A sparse set of long, parallel diagonal stripes specifies a periodic diagonal coloring. Infer which diagonal invariant is used (`r+c` for down-left/up-right stripes, or `r-c` for down-right/up-left stripes), infer the period and color for each residue from the stripe clues, then fill every cell with its corresponding color. Use zero-based row/column indices; keep the original grid dimensions.

This task's test has down-right stripes (constant `r-c`) and a period of 4. The complete mapping is:

- `(r-c) mod 4 = 0` → color `7`
- `(r-c) mod 4 = 1` → color `2`
- `(r-c) mod 4 = 2` → color `8`
- `(r-c) mod 4 = 3` → color `6`

Equivalently, `out[r][c] = mapping[(r-c) % 4]`. Verified against all visible test clues: the 8 stripe is residue 2; 2 stripe residue 1; 6 stripe residue 3; 7 stripe residue 0. Submitted the 12×12 periodic grid generated by this rule; evaluator confirmed CORRECT (0 wrong attempts).

Clues agree: sums 7→9, 28→4, 36→3, 39→7, and 40→8. This confirms the task family rule and that orientation determines whether to use sum or difference.

1. Identify stripe slope: constant `r+c` vs constant `r-c`.

3. Find the smallest consistent period (the four-color test instance has period 4; the demo has period 5), making sure distinct residues do not conflict.

# Continual-ARC task-9a8c4ac8 — rectangular frame fill

Solved and verified on 2026-10-20. The task shows hollow, axis-aligned rectangular/square frames on a uniform background. Fill each enclosed background cavity according to the parity of its side length (the inner cavity dimensions):

- Odd-width/odd-height cavity (examples: 1×1, 3×3, 5×5) → color 7.
- Even-width/even-height cavity (example: 2×2, 4×4) → color 2.

Leave the frame cells, surrounding background, and all other input pixels unchanged. All observed cavities had matching width/height parity (square cavities); no evidence for non-square/mixed-parity cavities, so do not extrapolate that case without a demo.

Demo evidence: background 5; cavities included a 1×1 inside color-8 frame → 7, 1×1 inside color-3 frame → 7, 5×5 inside color-1 frame → 7, and 2×2 cavities inside color-9, color-8, and color-8 frames → 2; 3×3 inside a color-1 frame → 7. Frame colors do not determine the fill.

Important: Do not fill every cavity with 7. The initial wrong submission did so for the 4×4 interior of the large color-6 frame; correcting that cavity to 2 made the submission correct. Identify the enclosed hole dimensions and preserve every non-cavity pixel exactly.

# Continual-ARC solved pattern: diagonal ray from a repeated 2x2 motif color

Observed and solved on task `task-b6c83d84` (1 wrong submission; 2 demo requests; test solved correctly). Useful recognition pattern: a 2x2 multicolor motif has one of its colors repeated at a diagonally adjacent external cell. Continue that repeated color in a straight diagonal ray outward from the 2x2 motif, starting beyond the external repeated-color cell and continuing toward the grid edge. Preserve all other cells/colors. If the ray outward is immediately clipped by the grid edge, the input can remain unchanged.

## Demos

- Demo 1: 26x24, background 8. Core 2x2 at rows 11-12, cols 10-11 (0-indexed): `[[9,6],[7,2]]`. Color 7 repeats outside at (13,9), diagonally down-left from the core's 7 at (12,10). Output adds 7 along the continuing down-left diagonal: (14,8), (15,7), ..., (22,0). Everything else is unchanged.
- Demo 2: 25x25, background 0. Core 2x2 at rows 14-15, cols 8-9: `[[6,5],[2,3]]`. Color 6 repeats outside at (13,7), diagonally up-left from the core's 6 at (14,8). Output adds 6 along the continuing up-left diagonal: (12,6), (11,5), ..., (6,0). Everything else is unchanged.

## Test and verification

Test is 23x6, background 1. Its 2x2 motif at rows 1-2, cols 4-5 is `[[3,2],[6,2]]`; color 3 repeats at (0,3), diagonally up-left from the motif's 3 at (1,4). The outward ray beyond (0,3) lies outside the grid, so output is exactly the unchanged input. This unchanged grid was confirmed CORRECT.

A wrong attempt changed test cell (2,5) from 2 to 3. Do not recolor or overwrite neighboring motif cells, and do not infer that a different color in the 2x2 block should be changed. The operation is to extend the repeated diagonal color only, outward away from the 2x2 motif.

# Continual-ARC task-b6c83d84 — diagonal ray pattern (instance ended unsolved)

**Important:** This instance reached the 8-submission attempt cap with every submission marked incorrect. Do not treat any candidate output below as confirmed. Earlier contents of this file claimed a different task and were wrong; this file replaces that mistaken note.

## Reusable rule inferred from demonstrations

A small multicolor 2x2 motif contains colors that recur on a diagonal just outside it. Extend each such matching-color diagonal ray outward from the motif, preserving the input and filling the continuation cells with that color (typically to the grid boundary). This can happen for multiple colors in the same instance. If no diagonal recurrence/continuation pattern is present, leave the grid unchanged. Identify the motif and the direction of each ray carefully; do not assume rays only go downwards or only one color extends.

Examples from this instance's demonstrations (coordinates 0-indexed):

- Demo 1, background 6: motif at rows 0–1, cols 8–9 = `[[8,8],[7,4]]`; matching 7 at (2,7) extends down-left through (9,0); matching 4 at (2,10) extends down-right through (11,19).
- Demo 2, background 9: motif rows 7–8, cols 12–13 = `[[8,4],[6,7]]`; 6 at (9,11) extends down-left to (12,8).
- Demo 3, background 3: motif rows 25–26, cols 0–1 = `[[8,9],[0,6]]`; 9 at (24,2) extends up-right through (18,8).

- Demo 7 has a 2x2 block `[[7,8],[4,2]]` without a matching diagonal repetition; output is unchanged.

The demonstrations show rays in different diagonal orientations. Preserve non-background motif cells; don't overwrite them.

# Continual-ARC task-eebc43a9 — solved 2026-10-20

## Reusable rule: move colored object against a full separator, then draw a perpendicular trailing line

The input contains a full-width or full-height separator line (color 2 in the observed demos), a uniform background, and an object/shape of another color. Translate the entire non-background object rigidly toward the separator until its nearest occupied edge is one cell away from the separator. Preserve its shape, color, and relative placement, including any disconnected pieces of that same object color. Remove it from its original location. Then draw a full grid-spanning line of color 8 perpendicular to the separator, one cell beyond the object's far edge (on the side the object was moved into). Keep the original separator unchanged.

Interpretation: the divider establishes the direction/side for sliding; object moves to just beyond it, and a perpendicular color-8 line is drawn immediately after the object's complete bounding extent. The shape is not filled or otherwise transformed.

## Evidence from demos

- Demo 1 (30x22): background 4; horizontal separator row 8, color 2. A 3x2 color-9 rectangle at rows 14–16, columns 5–6 moved upward to rows 9–11, same columns. The original rectangle disappeared. Full horizontal color-8 line was drawn at row 12. Separator row 8 remained color 2.
- Demo 2 (19x19): background 6; vertical separator column 2, color 2. Color-9 block at rows 0–4, columns 8–13 moved left to rows 0–4, columns 3–8. Original block disappeared. Full vertical color-8 line was drawn at column 9. Separator column 2 remained color 2.

## Solved test

Input 14x26: background 0; horizontal color-2 separator row 0; color-1 pattern occupies rows 4–8 and columns 3–8 (including a separate cell at row 5, column 8). Translate all color-1 cells upward by 3 rows, giving rows 1–5; preserve columns and exact pattern. Draw a full horizontal color-8 line at row 6. Rows 7–13 remain background. This exact grid was accepted.

## Practical procedure

1. Identify the uniform background and full separator row/column.
2. Find the other-color object(s) that belong to the movable pattern and compute its extent in the axis perpendicular to the separator. Preserve every cell of that color relative to the rest.
3. Translate the pattern toward the separator until its near edge has exactly one blank cell between it and the separator.
4. Put color 8 across the entire perpendicular row/column immediately beyond the pattern's far edge, on the same side of the separator.
5. Leave the old location as background and keep the separator unchanged. Check output dimensions and all unaffected cells.

# Continual-ARC task 01f3a263 — verified rule and solved instance

## Rule from the two demonstrations and accepted test
A grid contains two equal-sized panels separated by a solid line. The separator's orientation tells how to split and align the panels: with a vertical line, compare left/right cells at the same row and local column; with a horizontal line, compare top/bottom cells at the same local row and column. Find the single color shared by the two panels (in these examples, each panel otherwise has its own distinct background/color). The output has the paired-panel dimensions, is filled with that shared color, and has a `3` exactly at positions where BOTH aligned input cells have that shared color.

In concise form, for shared color `s`:
`out[r][c] = 3 if panelA[r][c] == s and panelB[r][c] == s else s`.

# Continual-ARC solved rule: recolor complete uniform grid lines (task-c25b713c)

**Verified by correct test submission with zero wrong attempts.**

Find any row or column that is entirely the same color (the line color). Recolor every cell belonging to each such complete row or column to color `2`. Preserve all other cells exactly as they were. If a cell belongs to both a qualifying row and column, it is still simply `2`.

The complete line color varies by instance; do not assume a particular input color. A line must span the full grid dimension. Do not recolor partial stripes or scattered cells of that color merely because they match the line color.

2. Mark all qualifying rows and columns before modifying anything.

# Continual-ARC task-de03619c — learned rule

Observed demonstration and solved test from 2026-10-20.

## Rule
The grid contains two same-sized binary-pattern panels separated by a straight divider of color 1. In the observed demo, panels were stacked with a full horizontal divider row of 4; in the test, panels were side-by-side with a full vertical divider column of 1. Treat color 3 as marked/foreground in both panels. Produce a grid matching the panel dimensions: put color 2 exactly where BOTH panels contain color 3 (cellwise intersection); put 0 elsewhere. The output corresponds to the first/top or left panel's alignment. Divider is excluded.

Equivalent: output[r][c] = 2 iff first_panel[r][c] == 3 and second_panel[r][c] == 3, else 0.

## Evidence
Demo 1: 29x11 input was two 14x11 panels separated by row 14 of color 4. The lower panel was an almost-all-1 mask with one zero at local row 7, column 8. Output was 14x11; top-panel 1s became 2s, except the location masked by that zero, supporting cellwise intersection. (The separator color differed in this demo.)

Test: 4x9 input had left/right 4x4 panels separated by column 4 of color 1. Applying the color-3 intersection rule yields:
[[0,0,0,2],
 [0,2,2,0],
 [0,0,0,0],
 [0,2,0,0]]
This exact submission was marked CORRECT.

If this task recurs, solve directly without requesting a demo unless panel layout or colors materially differ.

# Continual-ARC task-de03619c — solved rule (2026-10-20)

## Rule
The input has two equal-sized panels separated by a straight divider. Select the panel containing sparse color-8 marks (in the observed instances it is the left panel; the demo is also side-by-side). Output a grid the size of that panel: replace each 8 in the selected panel with 2, and make every other cell 0. Ignore the other panel's contents, including its background and holes. Exclude the divider.

For the observed left/right layout: `output[r][c] = 2 if left_panel[r][c] == 8 else 0`.

## Demonstration evidence
Demo input was 8x7: three-column left panel, separator column of 4, three-column right panel mostly color 5 with some 0s. Output was 8x3 and exactly mapped each 8 in the left panel to 2, leaving its 0s as 0. The right-panel 0s did not mask or otherwise alter the output.

## Solved test evidence
Test input was 17x25: 12-column left panel of 0/8 marks, separator column of 1, and 12-column right panel mostly 6 with sparse 0s. Correct output was 17x12, obtained by mapping each left-panel 8 to 2 and all left-panel 0s to 0. The exact output rows (each 12 cells) were:

```text
000000000000
000000000000
020000002000
000000002000
200000000200
000000000020
000002020022
000002000000
202200000000
000000000000
000020200220
000000000000
000000000000
002000000000
000000000000
000000000002
000020000200
```

This exact output was marked CORRECT.

## Pitfall
The first two submissions were incorrect because the 8 coordinates were shifted/mis-copied across rows, not because the rule required combining the two panels. Preserve the selected panel's original row/column alignment exactly. Do not infer a cellwise intersection with the opposite panel. No further demo is needed for a recurrence with the same clear 8-mark panel and separator layout.

# Continual-ARC puzzle note: hollow rectangular frames

Observed recurring rule from solved instance task-9a8c4ac8 (verified correct): find closed, axis-aligned rectangular outlines; fill their interior cells, leaving the outline and background unchanged. The fill color depends on the parity of the number of interior cells (interior area = (height-2)*(width-2)): odd area -> color 7; even area -> color 2.

Evidence across demos:
- 5x5 interior (25, odd) -> 7; 3x3 interior (9, odd) -> 7; single-cell interior (1, odd) -> 7.
- 2x2 interior (4, even) -> 2; 4x5 interior (20, even) -> 2.
- Solved test had a 6x6 interior (36, even) filled 2, 3x3 and 1x1 interiors filled 7; submitted answer was confirmed correct.

Use this as a hypothesis for related instances, verifying each candidate is a fully closed rectangular frame before filling. Do not recolor frame or background. Demonstration pairs showed frame colors/backgrounds vary and are not themselves the fill-color key; interior-area parity matched the fill color.

# Continual-ARC: object adjacent to vertical divider

Observed rule from solved task-eebc43a9:

- Background fills the grid; a full-height vertical line of color 2 is the divider.
- A colored object/pattern lies to the right of the divider. Identify its bounding box (ignore the divider/background).
- Translate the entire object's pattern horizontally so the left edge of its bounding box is immediately one column to the right of the divider, preserving all rows, colors, holes, and shape.
- Erase the object's original location (restore background there).
- Draw a full-height vertical line of color 8 immediately to the right of the translated object's bounding box.
- Keep grid dimensions and divider unchanged. The object may occupy only some rows; the new color-8 marker spans the full grid height.

Evidence from demonstrations:
1. 20x27, background 7, divider col 4, object bbox cols 16-17 (6 pattern). Output moves its pattern to cols 5-6 and puts full-height 8 at col 7.
2. 24x8, background 3, divider col 1, a 1-wide color-1 segment at col 3 rows 19-21. Output moves it to col 2 (same rows), clears col 3, and draws full-height 8 at col 3.

Solved test: 28x18, background 6, divider col 6, rectangle color 9 at rows 1-13, cols 11-14 (0-indexed). Output moves the rectangle to rows 1-13, cols 7-10, clears its source, and draws color 8 down col 11.

Indexing note: all column and row indices above are zero-based. The simple operational rule is: preserve the object’s internal shape; slide its bounding box flush against the divider’s right side; mark the next column after the object with 8 from top to bottom.

# Continual-ARC rule: horizontal marker gaps

Observed in task-b21aa0a0: on a uniform background, horizontal runs of color 7 with markers in every other column are completed by changing each intervening background cell between adjacent 7s to color 2. Preserve all 7 markers and all other cells; do not extend beyond either endpoint. A demonstration showed this for runs of 2–5 markers, and the test confirmed the rule simultaneously on separated rows with different run lengths. Useful approach: detect horizontal adjacent 7s separated by exactly one cell and recolor only the middle cell to 2.

# Continual-ARC: horizontal stripe sequence (observed)

This task turns a grid of full-width, solid-color horizontal stripes separated by 0 rows into a full grid of the same dimensions whose rows repeat a short cycle of stripe colors.

Observed demonstrations (0-based row indices):
- Demo 1: stripes `(6:4, 7:8, 9:6, 14:3, 22:6, 23:5)`. Sorting these stripes by `row_index mod 6` gives the 6-row cycle `[4, 8, 3, 6, 6, 5]`, repeated down all 27 rows.
- Demo 2: `(0:3, 5:7, 10:5, 13:3, 20:1, 21:3)`. Sorting by `row_index mod 6` gives `[3, 3, 1, 3, 5, 7]`, repeated down all 27 rows.

Practical rule supported by demos: identify the stripe colors, order them by their vertical position modulo 6 (residue 0 through 5), and repeat that six-color sequence over the output height; each output row is filled entirely with its cycle color. If a residue has multiple candidate stripes or others are extra, demos do not specify tie-breaking—inspect the solved example below rather than assuming the simple one-per-residue case.

Solved instance evidence: input 22x22 had stripes at zero-based rows `2:9, 12:2, 15:4, 17:9, 18:7, 20:6, 21:6`. Correct output repeated cycle `[6,4,9,9,7,2]` for 22 rows. This case has duplicate residue candidates and seven stripes, so the exact selection/tie rule remains uncertain; nevertheless the listed cycle is verified correct for that configuration.

# Continual-ARC: expand singleton markers into a line template

Observed recurring ARC transformation pattern (task-016ffa36): a sparse field contains many isolated marker cells plus one explicit short colored line template. Replace each marker by a copy of the template, centered so the marker occupies the template's center cell; preserve the background and original template. Extend in the template's orientation, keeping the line's color order. Check for overlaps and grid boundaries.

Evidence from the solved instance:
- Demo: background 9, isolated 8s, template `[2,1,6]` horizontally on one row. Each 8 became the center color 1, with 2 on its left and 6 on its right.
- Test: background 6, isolated 3s, template `[7,7,1]` vertically in one column. Each 3 became the center 7, with 7 above and 1 below. Submission was confirmed correct.

Practical method: identify background, template sequence/direction, and center marker color; scan original grid for isolated markers; replace each with the centered line, preserving all unrelated cells. If a marker would make the line extend off-grid, infer clipping only if the examples establish it.

# Continual-ARC: object moves toward a colored divider and leaves a line

Observed task `task-eebc43a9` (solved correctly after 2 demo requests). Likely reusable rule for this task family:

- The grid has a uniform background, a full straight divider in color 2, and a colored object on one side of it.
- Move the object (preserving its shape and color) along the axis perpendicular to the divider toward it, as far as possible until it is adjacent to the divider. If already adjacent, leave it in place.
- Add a full-length line in color 8 immediately on the object's opposite/trailing side, parallel to the divider. Keep the original divider and background unchanged.
- Keep the original grid dimensions.

Evidence from demos:
1. Demo 1: 17x22, background 9, horizontal color-2 divider at row 3, singleton color-5 object initially at (row 10, col 16). Output moves the singleton to (4,16), adjacent below divider, and adds a full color-8 row at row 5 (one row behind the moved object). Divider stays at row 3.
2. Demo 2: 22x22, background 7, vertical color-2 divider at column 20. A color-4 object at columns 18-19 is already adjacent, so stays put; output adds a full color-8 column at column 17. Divider stays at column 20.
3. Test grid (18x22), background 5, horizontal divider at row 15, color-7 shape in rows 7-12. Correct output translated the shape down two rows to rows 9-14 so it touched the divider, and added a full color-8 row at row 8. The submission was confirmed correct.

Practical check: identify the color-2 full row/column and object side; compute the tightest translation that brings the object's nearest extent next to the divider; place color 8 in the full parallel line immediately outside the object's far extent after translation.

# Continual-ARC lesson: noisy 2× expansion

Evidence from task-069823a2 (2026-10-21): Inputs were noisy grids; demonstrations showed output dimensions exactly doubled and the original input preserved unchanged in the upper-left quadrant. The other three quadrants looked noisy and did not support simple rotations/reflections; three geometric-copy submissions were wrong. The accepted 30×30 output for the 15×15 test was the unchanged input in the upper-left, with the dominant input color (4) filling every remaining cell.

Heuristic only, not a proven universal task rule: when demos show a doubled grid with noisy added regions and no stable transform, test a candidate that preserves the input upper-left and fills extensions with the dominant/background color. Do not assume rotated or reflected copies without demo verification. This instance's demos were noisy/nonuniform, so modal fill succeeded here but should be treated cautiously; verify against more evidence whenever possible.

# Continual-ARC reusable observations

## Verified instance: task-3caaa5de (solved 2026-10-20)

**Observed rule for this instance:** The test grid had background colors `0` and `5`, plus a three-cell vertical object of color `1` at rows 4–6, column 11 (1-indexed). The output paints color `1` onto every location belonging to a vertical run of three consecutive `0` cells, retaining the original grid everywhere else. Overlapping runs are unioned; do not mutate the source while discovering matches. The exact verified approach is: scan each column for every window of three rows whose original values are all `0`; set those three output cells to `1`.

**Important orientation detail:** A submission that also marked horizontal triples was incorrect. The vertical-only rule was confirmed correct. Do not assume rotation is allowed merely because it might be plausible for other object shapes; use demonstrations to establish the matching orientation.

**Attempt history / caution:** Several wrong attempts resulted from speculation and manually assembled grids. The decisive method was to compute matches against an immutable copy of the original input, union all hit cells, and preserve every unmarked cell. A vertical-only output was accepted after 5 wrong submissions. The background's more frequent color is not necessarily the target; here the matching cells were specifically `0`, and the recolor was the marker color `1`.

**Potential generalization (tentative, not proven for all shapes):** These instances appear to place copies of a small colored object onto matching zero-valued locations in a noisy two-color grid. Extract the object's shape/color, test translated placements using demonstrations, preserve orientation unless evidence permits transforms, and recolor only the matching footprint. Keep this as a hypothesis rather than assuming arbitrary zero triples or rotations in a new instance.

# Continual-ARC reusable observations

## Separator-panel count task (verified 2026-10-20; task-2dc37cc6)
A grid is partitioned by full horizontal and vertical separator lines (separator color is distinct). Treat each resulting rectangular panel independently. Each panel has a common background color and sparse occurrences of a second/speckle color. Produce a smaller grid with one output cell per panel, preserving panel row/column order. Output `1` for a panel containing **exactly two speckle cells**; otherwise output that panel's background color. Do not alter separators or copy the original panel contents.

Evidence: three demos and the test confirmed this. Demo 1 panels were 4x2 (output 2x5), background 2, speckles 9; only one panel had exactly two speckles, all others including the one-speckle top-left kept background 2. Demo 2 panels were 4x3 (output 3x2), background 9, speckles 4; exactly the two panels with two speckles output 1. Demo 3 panels were 5x4 (output 3x4), background 6, speckles 5; only the bottom-row, second-column panel had two speckles, so it output 1. Verified test task-2dc37cc6: separators were rows 3,7 and cols 4,9 (0-based), yielding 3x3 panels each 3x4; background 6 and speckle 5. Exactly-two-speckle panels yielded the accepted output:
`[[1,6,1],[6,1,6],[1,1,1]]`.

Procedure: identify complete separator rows/columns; extract panels between them; count cells of the sparse non-background color in each panel; mark exactly-count-2 with 1, otherwise use background color. Check boundaries/counts carefully. This same rule can be inferred when dimensions or palette vary.

## Fill enclosed background regions
A demonstrated transformation: identify any region of background color enclosed by a connected boundary/object of another color, and recolor the enclosed area **4**. Leave the boundary/object and all exterior background unchanged. In the example, color-6 contours enclosed color-7 cavities; those cavities became 4. In the solved instance, a color-7 rectangular frame enclosed color 5, which became 4, while the external color-5 and the frame's external stem stayed unchanged.

# Continual-ARC: overlap of panels separated by a uniform line

Observed across task-de03619c (7 demos): a full-width uniform separator row or full-height uniform separator column divides the grid into two equal-sized panels. The separator color itself can vary (examples: 3, 7, 9). Compare corresponding cells in the two panels; output has the dimensions of one panel and contains color 2 exactly where both corresponding cells are nonzero, and 0 otherwise. Ignore the foreground colors when testing overlap; they may differ between panels. This is a pixelwise logical AND of nonzero masks, rendered as 2.

The panels can be arranged horizontally or vertically. For a horizontal divider, use rows above and below it; for a vertical divider, use columns left and right. Verify corresponding panel dimensions and align coordinates directly. Examples included different foreground colors and sparse/noisy masks; overlap rule reproduced the outputs.

Narrow test example from this task: input was 9x2, with row 4 `[7,7]` acting as horizontal separator. Top panel rows 0-3 and bottom panel rows 5-8 each have size 4x2. Only top row 3 `[5,5]` overlaps bottom row 3 (input row 8) `[0,5]`, so output is `[[0,0],[0,0],[0,0],[0,2]]`.

When the input has this clear equal-panel separator and the demos establish the overlap rule, submit directly; avoid unnecessary demo requests. Do not mistake a two-column test's separator row for another panel or compare the separator as part of either panel.

# Continual-ARC task family: panel encoding (observed task id task-2dc37cc6)

This task uses input grids partitioned by full-width horizontal separator rows and a full-height vertical separator column. Each rectangular panel yields one output cell, preserving panel order. In the observed demos, 23x9 inputs had four rows of panels by two columns (5x4 data panels, with separators); output was 4x2. The test was 8x5 with three rows by two columns (2x2 data panels); output was 3x2.

Do not assume simple dot-count coding: examples contradict that. Demo 1 background=5, marker=2; output 4x2 was [[1,1],[1,1],[1,1],[1,5]]. Most panels had two markers and output 1, while a one-marker panel yielded 5. Demo 2 background=3, marker=8; output was [[1,1],[1,1],[3,1],[1,1]]. One-marker panels yielded different values (3 vs 1), so the marker's position/pattern likely matters too. The solved test used background-like colors 2 and 3 with separator 9 and output [[1,1],[3,3],[1,3]].

Practical strategy for future instances: identify separators, split into panels, compare each panel's non-background cells (count and within-panel positions) to outputs from demos. Track exact positions as well as counts; don't infer a count-only rule. Request a demo if the task repeats with insufficient examples. Existing evidence includes only two demo pairs and one solved test, so this is a task-family clue, not a fully established rule.

# Continual-ARC task pattern: task-2dc37cc6

## Inferred rule (confirmed by demos and successful test)
The input is a rectangular array of same-background rectangular compartments, separated by full rows/columns of a separator color. Each compartment contains marker pixels of one distinct color. Produce a compact grid with one output cell per compartment, preserving the compartment row/column layout. For each compartment:
- If it contains **exactly two** marker pixels, output color **1**.
- Otherwise (0, 1, or more than 2 markers), output that compartment's background color.

In all observed demos compartments had the same background and marker colors within the puzzle; derive those from the non-separator, non-marker cells, rather than hard-coding colors. Output has number of compartment rows × number of compartment columns.

## Evidence from demos
- Demo 1: separator 6, background 3, marker 7; four compartment rows × three columns. Exactly-two marker compartments output 1; others output 3.
- Demo 2: separator 4, background 5, marker 9; five × five compartments. Output 1 at compartments with exactly two markers; other compartments output 5.
- Demo 3: separator 3, background 5, marker 8; four × two compartments. Exactly-two marker compartments output 1; all others output 5.
- Test solved correctly with one wrong attempt: separator 6, background 4, marker 8; output `[[1,1,1,1],[1,4,1,1],[1,1,4,1]]`.

## Practical solving procedure
1. Identify full separator rows and columns, then split into compartments.
2. Identify marker and background colors from a compartment.
3. Count marker cells in each compartment.
4. Emit 1 iff count equals 2; otherwise emit background color. Verify output dimensions and counts before submission.

Important: a previous incorrect submission used color 3 for the non-two-marker case by overfitting demo 1. The rule is to use the compartment's actual background color, which changes across tasks/demos.

# Continual-ARC task 89695a26 transformation

Observed from two demos (3x5 -> 9x10 and 9x3 -> 27x6) and confirmed by successful test submission (6x15 -> 18x30):

For an input grid with H rows and W columns, output has 3H rows and 2W columns. Transform each source row by concatenating its horizontal reversal with the original row (`row[::-1] + row`). The output's source-row order is: all input rows reversed (bottom to top), then all rows in original order (top to bottom), then all rows reversed again (bottom to top). Equivalently, each of three vertical bands is an H-row sequence: reversed, forward, reversed. No cell colors are changed.

Example: input row [a,b,c] -> [c,b,a,a,b,c]. For input rows A,B,C, output row source sequence is C,B,A,A,B,C,C,B,A.

This is an evidence-based reusable rule for this task family; verify dimensions/row lengths before submitting. The first incorrect attempt in the instance was based on an incorrect guessed pattern and wrong dimensions; the successful answer used the rule above.

# Continual-ARC learned task rule: task-89695a26

Observed demo: a 5x14 input grid mapped to a 15x28 output grid. Output preserves every original cell's color and replaces each cell with a solid 3-row by 2-column block of that color (nearest-neighbor scaling; height ×3, width ×2).

Verified test: input was 6x2, all cells 8. Correct output was 18x4, all cells 8. For future recurrences of this task, expand each input cell to a 3×2 block, preserving its value.

# Continual-ARC task-89695a26: row reflection + vertical bands

## Verified rule from this instance's two demos
For input grid H×W, output is 3H×2W. For every input row `r`, form the widened row `reverse(r) + r` (horizontal mirror followed by original; do NOT duplicate each individual cell). Then concatenate row sequences for three vertical bands: input rows bottom-to-top, input rows top-to-bottom, then input rows bottom-to-top. No colors change.

Equivalent pseudocode:
```
wide = [row[::-1] + row for row in input]
output = [wide[i] for i in reversed(range(H))] + wide + [wide[i] for i in reversed(range(H))]
```

## Evidence
Demo 1 input 9×1 `[7,5,8,9,5,0,3,1,5]` yields 27×2: reversed rows `[5,1,3,0,5,9,8,5,7]` duplicated across width; then forward input `[7,5,8,9,5,0,3,1,5]` duplicated; then reversed again.
Demo 2 input 1×15 `[8,1,8,7,8,8,0,0,8,8,8,1,8,8,4]` yields 3 identical rows, each `reverse(input row) + input row`, confirming horizontal reverse-and-concatenate (not per-cell scaling).

## Pitfalls observed
Eight test submissions were incorrect. The repeated mistake was width expansion by duplicating every cell (`a,a,b,b,...`) and guessing vertical bands/row orders inconsistently. Correct horizontal operation reverses the full row then appends the original. For test grid 5×10, expected dimensions are 15×20. The rule is grounded in the demos, but no test submission was correct in this instance; prioritize this exact demonstrated transform if the task recurs.

# Continual-ARC task patterns

## 18x18 mosaic -> 6x6 color map (demonstrated 2026-10-20, task-60c42a29)
When the 18x18 input is partitioned into 3x3 tiles, create a 6x6 output. For each tile, output its distinct foreground color (e.g. 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9) if present; output 0 if the tile contains no foreground color. In the demonstrated examples, 0 and 5 are tile background/blank colors, and each nonblank tile has a single foreground color (often arranged as a small symbol/pattern). Tile position is preserved. The 18x18 test was solved correctly with this extraction rule.

# Continual-ARC learned patterns

## Hollow plus connectors (observed in task-fe4daa85)

A hollow plus object consists of four color-2 cells at the cardinal neighbors of an empty center. When two such plus centers share a row or column, connect their facing outer arms with color 1: fill every cell strictly between the facing color-2 arm endpoints, leaving the pluses themselves unchanged. In practice, this fills the intervening axis including the blank centers. Handle every aligned pair independently; preserve all other cells.

Evidence: in the demo, hollow-plus centers at (row 1, col 3) and (row 1, col 10) were linked horizontally with 1s in columns 5–8; centers at (row 1, col 10) and (row 5, col 10) were linked vertically at (row 3, col 10). In the solved test, centers (2,2) and (6,2) linked vertically at (4,2), and centers (6,2) and (6,10) linked horizontally across columns 4–8 (zero-based coordinates). This supports connecting only row/column-aligned hollow pluses, not diagonal pairs.

# Continual-ARC task-92aa891e

Solved from one demonstration (0 wrong submissions; 1 demo request). Useful reusable rule for this task family:

- A background grid (color 1 in these examples) is divided into equal-sized rectangular tiles by full separator lines (color 4 here).
- Find the non-background motif inside the one tile that contains it, ignoring divider lines.
- Copy that motif, preserving its relative cell positions and colors, into every tile; leave background cells as background and separator lines unchanged.
- In the demo (11x5), separators were row 3 and column 2; the 3x2 motif from the upper-left tile was copied into all six tiles.
- In the solved test (17x11), separators were rows 5 and 11 and columns 3 and 7; the 3x3 motif in the middle-left tile was repeated in all nine tiles. Motif positions in local tile coordinates: (0,2)=7, (1,0)=9, (2,1)=7.

General caution: detect tile dimensions from full separator lines and locate the unique motif-bearing tile; it need not be the top-left tile. Copy only the motif, not the source tile's background.

# Continual-ARC learned pattern

## Recoloring complete monochrome lines
A demonstrated task pattern: find the color that fills entire rows and/or entire columns in the grid, then recolor those complete uniform lines to color 2. Do not recolor isolated occurrences of that same color elsewhere; preserve all other cells. In the demo, uniform rows and columns of color 4 became 2, while scattered 4s remained. In the solved test, complete rows/column of color 8 became 2, while scattered 8s remained. This is a reusable hypothesis for similar future tasks, not a certainty for unrelated grids; request a demo if unclear.

# Continual-ARC learned rule: recolor 5 to the other color

Observed and verified in task-0af76fdb (three examples, one test solved): grids contain exactly color 5 plus one other color. ## Rule
The input is an enlarged lattice: a regular set of horizontal and vertical separator lines surrounds large uniform interior areas. Identify the repeated line coordinates and the uniform interior/fill color. Finally, trim the candidate output to the tight bounding box of cells that differ from the fill color. Preserve a 1x1 output when that is the remaining box.

In these examples the line crossings can be read where the periodic horizontal and vertical separator bands intersect. The broad regions between them are uniform fill. **Outcome:** attempt cap reached: 8 incorrect submissions, 8 demo requests. Do not treat any test candidate below as correct. This task ID has recurred with apparently related line-bridging tasks and also a rectangular-outline variant, so use fresh demos rather than relying on ID alone.

## What demos established with strong evidence
Transformation adds color 2 into some 9-cells on horizontal/vertical straight segments involving 8 markers. Basic successful-looking cases include ordinary interpolated gaps; e.g. demo 8 row 0 fills between multiple 0 endpoints, vertical gaps fill in repeated columns, and row/column intersections are possible. Demos 4-7 contain long vertical/horizontal runs with interrupted marker cells and background gaps. Demos 1 is an already-complete rectangular border and unchanged.

Caution: a naive “fill every gap between any two collinear markers” produced plausible outputs but failed repeatedly on this test. The following hypotheses were each tested and evaluator-rejected in some form: all collinear interpolation (including all row and column pairs), broad rectangular interior/perimeter fill, omit long horizontal fills, omit horizontal fills on rows with only two markers, and a short/filtered subset of vertical bridges. Thus the exact selection rule was not recovered. Do not repeat a blanket interpolation rule or infer success from demos alone.

Some demonstration outputs contain apparent exceptions that should be analyzed before applying a generic interpolation rule:
- Demo 2 input/output: marker 7 on bg 1, row 3 has markers c10,c12,c13,c15,c16,c17; output fills c11 and c14; vertical gaps in c10/c17 are filled. Row 11 has markers c10,c13,c15,c16,c17; output fills c11,c12,c14.
- Demo 4: marker 8 on bg 7, long vertical rails at c0,c3,c7; only gap cells on those aligned rails are changed; unrelated wide horizontal spaces remain untouched.
- Demo 5: marker 7 on bg 3, long gaps are interpolated, including horizontal r8 c3-c6 and vertical repeated-column gaps.
- Demo 6: marker 8 on bg 4, output fills vertical c0 and c12 from r0 to r7 and horizontal row 7 between c0 and c12, including long stretches.
- Demo 7: marker 8 on bg 0, output bridges missing cells on vertical rails c2/c8 and the top/bottom horizontal bars; many possible collinear spans are filled.
- Demo 8: marker 0 on bg 1, output fills many horizontal and vertical gaps with 2. There is an apparent extension/anomaly at r13,c14 (input there is 1; output 2), and earlier demo 2 also had an unexplained cell just beyond a marker run. These may be clues to a line continuation/bounding geometry rule.

## Failed test submissions (conceptual summary)
1. Full interpolation for all row/column marker pairs, plus multiple long bridges; rejected.
2. Substantially same, with attempt to correct vertical extrapolation; rejected.
3. Same collinear interpolation regenerated; rejected.
4. Added a completed bounding rectangle-like outline from marker extrema and additional bottom-row horizontal fills; rejected.
5. Tried a restricted version without long row2/row6 horizontal spans, retaining some vertical/bottom fills; rejected.
6. Returned to full interpolation; rejected.
7. Tried a narrowed “no horizontal row2/row6 fill” variant with vertical bridge fills and bottom gap; rejected.
8. Tried a variant retaining horizontal fills on rows 2/6, plus vertical fills and bottom bridge; rejected.

These failures show that the issue is not simply one transcription error or whether the two long horizontal spans are included; several near-equivalent fill patterns failed. In particular, repeated submission of any straightforward all-collinear-gap candidate is not productive.

## Useful follow-up approach for future recurrence
1. Inspect the full demos cell-by-cell and enumerate every change, not just representative examples; infer a geometric criterion that explains both the anomalous extensions and unfilled alignments.
2. Determine whether markers define specific strokes/rectangular segments or a boundary-bounded region, and whether only a subset of marker lines qualify. Check every candidate rule against every demo before submitting.
3. Use exact input transcription and script-generated outputs; retain unchanged background except where a demonstrated rule justifies changes.
